title: Make the bytecode tracer agree with the JVM on increments

blocks.text: A code-review bot explains suspicious arithmetic by running the bytecode javac produced for a method and printing what it returns, so a reviewer can see why `total = total++ + bonus` doesn't do what it looks like. Its interpreter, `IntMachine`, reads instructions as `javap -c` prints them. Loads, stores and constants already work; two pieces don't.
When you're done, every method the tests feed it returns exactly what the JVM returned when it ran the same method. About eight lines in total.
The tests hold each program next to the Java method javac compiled it from, and compare the two results.

cases.says: a method of loads, multiplications and additions returns what the JVM returns
a post-increment inside an expression contributes the value loaded before the increment
subtraction and division use the earlier-loaded value as the left operand
a compound assignment or decrement changes the local by the amount it names

origin.section: Bytecode Works on an Operand Stack, So `i = i++` Stores the Old Value Back

concepts: Arithmetic instructions pop the right operand first: isub subtracts the top of the stack from the value under it, which was loaded earlier.
i++ pushes the variable's old value before iinc changes the local, so i = i++ stores the old value back and an expression that uses i++ sees the value before the increment.
